o: We maintain an unbounded row of bounded stacks. `push` must fill the **leftmost** non-full stack, `pop` must take from the **rightmost** non-empty stack, and `popAtStack(index)` operates on one specific stack. The example shows the key subtlety: after `popAtStack(0)` frees a slot in an early stack, a later `push(20)` must go back into index 0 rather than creating a new rightmost stack. With up to 2·10^5 operations and indices up to 10^5, any solution that scans all stacks per operation (O(n) per call) is borderline but workable; however, we can do better by tracking candidate indices in ordered structures so each operation is near O(log n).
k: Only the leftmost non-full stack matters for push, and only the rightmost non-empty stack matters for pop — maintain sorted sets/heaps of such indices instead of scanning.
A min-heap of 'not-full' indices plus a max view of existing indices handles push/pop in O(log n); popAtStack just re-inserts its index into the not-full heap.
Lazy cleanup: when popping from the rightmost stack, drop trailing empty stacks so the structure doesn't grow without bound.

a.i: Keep a simple list of stacks. For push, scan left to right for the first stack with size < capacity (creating one if none exists). For pop, scan right to left for the first non-empty stack. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is easy to reason about; it passes because operation counts are modest, though each call may be O(number of stacks).
s: Store stacks in a dynamic array `stks`, each a list capped at capacity.
push: find first index with len < capacity; if none, append a new stack; append val.
popAtStack(i): if i out of range or stack empty return -1, else pop top.
pop: scan from last stack backwards to first non-empty, pop its top; return -1 if none.
a.t: O(S) per operation where S is the number of stacks created (up to O(n)); total worst case O(n^2), acceptable for n = 2·10^5 only because S stays small in practice.
a.sp: O(total elements stored) for the stacks themselves.

a.n: Approach 2: Min-Heap of Available Indices + Lazy Cleanup (Optimal)
a.i: Maintain a min-heap containing indices of stacks that are known to have free space. Push pops the smallest valid index from the heap (validating against current sizes since entries can go stale). Pop uses the last stack in the array, trimming empty trailing stacks. popAtStack pushes its index back into the heap after removal. Each heap entry is pushed at most once per capacity-slot event, giving amortized logarithmic cost.
s: Keep `stks` as a list of lists and a min-heap `free` of indices with size < capacity.
push: pop stale entries (index >= len(stks) or full); if heap empties, create a new stack at index len(stks); append val there.
pop: trim trailing empty stacks; if none remain return -1; pop top of last stack and push its index onto `free`.
popAtStack(i): validate bounds/emptiness, pop top, push i onto `free`.
All heap operations are O(log n); stale entries are discarded lazily on pop.
a.t: O(log n) amortized per operation — each push/pop does O(1) heap ops, and every heap entry is inserted once and popped at most once.
a.sp: O(n) for the stored values plus heap entries (bounded by number of slots ever freed).

w: In an interview, start with Approach 1 to establish correctness, then optimize with the min-heap of free indices — interviewers expect the heap/set-based design given the topic tags. Common pitfalls: forgetting to discard stale heap entries whose stacks became full or were trimmed; forgetting to trim trailing empty stacks in `pop` (memory blow-up and wrong rightmost behavior); off-by-one errors when a freed index equals the current last stack. Edge cases: pushing into a hole created mid-row, popping from an empty structure repeatedly, and `popAtStack` on out-of-range or empty indices. Follow-ups might ask for a balanced BST / ordered set instead of a heap (to also support deletion of arbitrary indices) or making the structure persistent/concurrent.
